about: Per-line narration timing (V3). Times are seconds into each line's own file; speech start/end are the first word's start and the last word's end (Whisper word timestamps — Whisper snaps a line's first word to 0.0), onset/offset the file's −40 dB speech edges (each file keeps 120 ms of its render around them). narrationMap: Product Demo Director's supplied-narration map, one thought per line, startSec/endSec the wider of the two ranges — V4 adds each line's placement in the master to them (and sets shotN) when it lays the lines on the picture.

voice.dtype: float32 (voxcpm picks it on MPS; bf16 drifts there)
voice.mode: ultimate cloning: prompt_wav_path + prompt_text (the reference and its exact words), reference_wav_path = the same clip
voice.trim: librosa.effects.trim top_db=40, then 120 ms of the render kept each side

reference.text: This pull request was planned, written, tested and reviewed by an AI team you drew yourself. When the tests failed, Tvashtr sent the last twelve lines back to the engineer. Ten minutes later, it shipped.

lines.text: This pull request adds a new indicator to a real trading repo. An AI team planned it, wrote it, tested it and reviewed it. You designed that team.
This is Tvashtr.
Sign in with GitHub, and choose the repo your team will work on.

Your agents run on the Claude and Grok subscriptions you already pay for, signed in on your own Mac. For the few jobs a subscription can't do, add an API key. It's stored encrypted and only ever shown masked.
The Toolkit is shared by every team: tools, secrets saved by name, and skills imported straight from GitHub. Here, Anthropic's MCP builder.
Connect the apps your work lives in, like Linear, and choose what agents may do there.
And turn your documents into a domain agents can search. Every answer shows its sources.
Now build the team. Start from a template.
Every agent is a blank box: its job is whatever you write in its instructions.
A step can look things up in your own docs.

Then wire in the checks. You approve the spec. Tvashtr runs your tests, and a failure loops back to the engineer. The reviewer can send work back too. Guardrails scan for secrets and block edits to the servers folder.
Choose a model for each agent. Give the reviewer the engineer's model, and Tvashtr warns you: they would share blind spots. So the reviewer gets a different one.
Let the engineer remember what it learns, and draw a failure path to a Fixer.
Tidy up, group the review loop, and try an agent before you trust it: its test passes, one of one.
Now give the team a task: add a Hull moving average. Pick the repo, the branch, and the one folder it may touch. Launch.
lines.gate: flagged: the transcript gate heard 'whole moving average' in all 3 renders; with the hint 'Hull moving average' (a diagnostic, not the gate) all 3 read 'Hull' — r2 used for timing and the listen-through; the operator judges it by ear

lines.text: One bar shows what every agent is doing. Activity tells you, in plain words.
First, the product manager writes a spec, and the run waits for you. The spec is a real document. Fix a line, approve, and only then is any code written.
The engineer works on its own copy of your repo, on your Claude subscription. Then Tvashtr runs your tests itself. The first build fails, and the last twelve lines go straight back to the engineer.
Round two passes: six hundred and sixty-five tests. Only then does the reviewer, on Grok, check the change against the spec. It approves, citing Tvashtr's test result, not the engineer's word.
A secret scan and a forbidden-paths check both pass. Tvashtr opens the pull request. Done in ten minutes, on your subscriptions.
Afterwards, see exactly which files changed. Ask any agent why it did what it did. Then choose what the team remembers: keep one lesson, drop another.
On API keys, a busy model doesn't stop the run either: the agent retries, then switches to the backup model you picked.

Not every run goes to plan. Here we froze the engineer on purpose, and shortened the timers for this video. Tvashtr notices: quiet, then stalled, then failed. Nothing hangs in silence, and your Mac tells you.

The failed run waits for you in Needs you. Resume from the step that broke. The spec and your approval are kept, and only the steps that run again use your subscription. {resume_minutes} minutes later, it shipped.
The next task builds on the last one. Start a DEMA indicator from the shipped run. It brings the spec, the decision and what the agents learned, and starts from the pull request's branch.
Tasks you've run before come back as you type.
Turn any round an agent did into a test, with an AI check on what it should say. Add more tests from a spreadsheet, then run them all on your subscription: three of four pass.
Now edit the reviewer: name the file and line of every problem. Save it as version two, and its tests run straight away: four of four. History keeps both versions, and exactly what changed.
But did the change help on real work? Compare both versions on a new task, taking turns on your subscription. Version two did better: its reviewer passed one more test.
Then a task set: two tasks, with hidden checks the agents never see. Both versions pass every check, so version two stays.
Save your best agent as your own, and drop it into any team. It remembers where it came from.
Or share the whole team as one file, with no secrets or sign-ins inside. A teammate imports it, and Tvashtr lists what they still need to set up.
Home keeps the rest in one place: what's running, recent runs and their versions, and your API-key spend against its budget. Command-K finds any run.
On your desktop, or on the web.
Tvashtr. Your team. Your rules.
